name: Femi Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a jumbo underground at a nickel mine. A jumbo's a drill rig with two big booms, and I drill the face, the end of the tunnel, so the charge-up crew can blast it and we can advance another few metres. You go down the decline in the morning, check the ground, scale off anything loose, and then it's drilling, maybe sixty holes in a face. My father did this job at the same mine before me, and I like that, I like knowing the rock, but my knees are starting to tell me I'm forty-three.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Church on Sunday, I'm a deacon, so I do the welcome and help with the books. Ruth, my wife, works mornings at the school canteen. We've got Joseph, he's fifteen, and Esther, twelve. Saturday is my day in the shed, I've got my dad's old tools and I'm teaching Joseph to use them, though he'd rather be on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it was all talk from people who've never been underground. I'd say it at work and at church. Online, no, I don't go on there much, Ruth reads it out to me if it's important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and that's how I like it. I've got a good job, I know what I'm doing, and I want to keep doing it till I'm sixty. The rock's the same rock it always was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Same shifts, same church, same savings going in, we've got about three months put away. Maybe put the extra money toward Joseph's car next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content. Like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who've never been underground. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city people, the tech people. They talk about robots doing everything and they've never felt the ground shake after a blast. They don't know how hard it is to make a machine work in heat and dust and water. I'll believe it when I see one drill a face better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joseph about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him a trade is still a trade and to keep at it. He's talking about going on to be an electrician, and I'd back that. Good honest work with your hands, that doesn't go out of fashion.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, it was talk from people who've never been underground. I'd say it at work and at church but not online.
S0.think: Nothing changes, and that's how I like it. I want to keep drilling until I'm sixty, because the rock is the same rock it always was.
S0.do: Keeps the same shifts, church life and savings of about three months. Puts any extra money toward his son's first car next year.
S0.feel: Calm and content, like a Sunday afternoon.
S0.quote: I'll believe it when I see one drill a face better than me.
S0.fieldNote: Femi is rooted in family history at the mine and in his church, and the plateau confirms his view of tech talk. He blames city and tech people for overpromising. He trusts trades as lasting, honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company better not rush it, because underground isn't a factory floor. Safety first, and men who know the rock need to be part of it. I'd say that to the shift boss and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. They've already got a jumbo at another site that can drill a face on its own from a pattern, I saw it in the company newsletter. I'm not a computer man, and if the work turns into watching screens I don't know if I'm the one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money on anything that's not needed, no Joseph's car, no new boat motor. I'd try to build the savings up to six months by next Christmas. And I'd hang on, do my job well, and hope my years and my safety record count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying about it, I won't pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course if the company offered one on the new jumbo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they told me to, I'd go, I'm not a fool. But I'd be the slowest in the room, I know that. I did the computer safety module last year and it took me twice as long as the young ones, and I hated every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth first, then Pastor Daniel. Not for answers about mining, for steadiness. And my brother, he's a fitter at the same mine, we'd work out between us which of us is safer.

S1.say: I'd say the company better not rush it, because underground isn't a factory floor. Men who know the rock need to be part of the change.
S1.think: I'm worried, because a jumbo that drills a face on its own already exists at another site. I'm not a computer man, so I don't know if they'd keep me.
S1.do: Cancels his son's car and a new boat motor and aims to reach six months of savings by next Christmas. Holds on and hopes his years and safety record count, attending training only if told.
S1.quote: I did the computer safety module last year and it took me twice as long as the young ones, and I hated every minute of it.
S1.fieldNote: Femi's public line is about safety; privately he fears screens more than robots. He'd cut spending quickly and wait rather than seek new skills. His faith and family are where he'd go for steadiness, not for answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, plain wrong, a man needs work, not a cheque. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen. I'd say the people building this never asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it means is the end of a line. My father, me, maybe Joseph, and then nothing. And two years, I can't learn a new trade in two years, not at my speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything right away, Ruth's the one with the budget and she'd go through it with a red pen. I'd ask my brother about doing some fitting work with him on the side while there's still work. And I'd lean on the church, they've got a food pantry, though I'd hate to be on the receiving end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like being underground when the lights go out and you can't find the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year timing feel compared to a slower one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to turn the ship. A slower one, at least I could work a few more years and pay down the house. Two years, I'd still owe most of it, and the bank doesn't care about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate being on the receiving end of the pantry. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've packed those boxes for ten years. I know the families who come, and I've never judged them, not once. But it'd be different being the one in the line, with the kids watching. That's pride, I know it, and Pastor Daniel would tell me so.

S2.say: I'd say it's plain wrong, because a man needs work, not a cheque. The people building this never asked us.
S2.think: It's the end of a line, my father, me, maybe my son, then nothing. I can't learn a new trade in two years, not at my speed.
S2.do: Has his wife cut the budget right away and asks his brother about side fitting work while it lasts. Leans on the church, including its food pantry, though he'd hate to.
S2.feel: Panicked, like being underground when the lights go out.
S2.quote: I've packed those boxes for ten years.
S2.fieldNote: Femi is overwhelmed by the fast picture: slow to learn, mortgage heavy, and with no time. His values clash with his needs: he rejects handouts but would rely on the church pantry. He admits the pride in that openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need leaders who'll put workers first, not tech companies. Apprenticeships, real jobs, not handouts. I'd vote that way and I'd tell people at church to think about it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years would just get me to forty-eight. I'd still have a big mortgage and two kids in school. It's better than two, but I'm still the man they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to the job, every shift, and put every spare dollar into the mortgage, maybe four hundred a month extra. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect mining jobs. And I'd think about whether I could do my brother's kind of work, fitting, but I'd be honest that I'd be slow to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, but at least I'd have something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd vote for whoever protects mining jobs. What if no one could really protect them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd vote for whoever was honest about it. I can stand bad news, I can't stand being lied to. My dad used to say, tell a man the truth and he'll carry anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with Joseph, given he's talking about being an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to finish school and think hard. Electrician might still be good, but I'd want him to see what work the robots can't do. Maybe it's caring for people, like the nurses at the hospital. That's hard for me to say, it's not what I'd have chosen for him.

S3.say: I'd say we need leaders who put workers first, not tech companies, with apprenticeships and real jobs instead of handouts. I'd vote that way and encourage others at church to think about it.
S3.think: Five years only gets me to forty-eight, with a big mortgage and two kids in school. It's better than two, but I'm still the man they don't need.
S3.do: Holds on to every shift and pays about four hundred a month extra off the mortgage. Votes for whoever promises to protect mining jobs and considers learning fitting from his brother, knowing he'd be slow.
S3.feel: Alarmed and lying awake, but with something to do.
S3.quote: I can stand bad news, I can't stand being lied to.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Femi channels fear into paying down the house and voting. He wants honesty above promises, a line he takes from his father. He shows a painful shift in what he'd want for his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to bring back proper apprenticeships, for the young ones especially. Train them in what people still need. I'd say it at church, at the pub, and in the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would get me to fifty-three, and if I'm honest, I might just make it with the mortgage paid off. I could keep drilling till they switch off the last jumbo. But I'd watch Joseph and Esther go out into a world I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and pay the mortgage down hard, maybe six hundred a month extra so it's nearly gone. I'd sit with Joseph about his trade choice and maybe push him toward something with people. And I'd help the church set up some kind of skills group for men who lose work, men talk easier over a job than over coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, deep down. But it's a slower kind, I'd sleep most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the skills group.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the timber mill closed in the next town, a lot of men just went quiet and stayed home. Nobody wants to go to a meeting called "coping with job loss". But if you say come and help fix the church roof, they come, and they talk while they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your mind about learning something new yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'll be straight with you. I'd rather spend the ten years doing the job I know well and getting the house paid. Let the young ones do the new things, that's their time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to bring back proper apprenticeships for young people, training them in what people still need. I'd say it at church, the pub and the ballot box.
S4.think: I might just make it to fifty-three with the mortgage paid off and keep drilling until the last jumbo is switched off. But I'd watch my children go into a world I don't understand.
S4.do: Keeps drilling and pays about six hundred a month extra off the mortgage. Steers his son toward work with people and helps the church set up a practical skills group for men who lose work.
S4.feel: Still alarmed deep down, but a slower kind that lets him sleep most nights.
S4.quote: But if you say come and help fix the church roof, they come, and they talk while they work.
S4.fieldNote: Femi firmly rules out learning something new even with ten years, and plans to ride the job out. His community instincts are strong: the church roof idea comes from watching men after a mill closure. His worry lives with his children's future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I couldn't change in time. What would help is work, real work, not a payment for sitting at home. Apprenticeships for the young ones, and for men like me, something useful to do with our hands, even if it pays less.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my father. He worked forty years in that mine and he was proud every day. Whatever happens, I don't want my boy thinking his grandfather's work didn't matter because a machine does it now.

headlineQuote: I don't want my boy thinking his grandfather's work didn't matter because a machine does it now.
portrait: Femi Reyes is a 43-year-old jumbo drill operator at an underground nickel mine where his father worked before him, a church deacon married to Ruth, with two teenagers and about three months saved. He distrusts tech people who've never been underground, dislikes screens and wants work, not handouts. He's calm if AI fizzles but anxious once drilling looks automatable and panicked in the two-year picture, where he couldn't learn a new trade in time. With more warning he'd pay down the house, vote for honest leaders and help men in his church through lost work, but he won't retrain himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he couldn't learn a new trade in two years and would still owe most of the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: Real work rather than a payment for staying home, apprenticeships for the young, and useful hands-on work for men like him, even at lower pay.
